cap_meas: Measured (same high-rate run, a cap of 50 on the attention logits): held-out 2.845 against 4.295 uncapped and 2.432 with QK-norm; the largest raw logit before the cap reached 6,296. {%cap_say%}
cap_say: The cap helps but less than QK-norm: logits keep growing behind it (raw 6,296), but because no capped logit can exceed 50 no head goes fully one-hot (lowest layer entropy 1.371 nats against 0.004 uncapped). That is one reason Gemma 3 switched to QK-norm, which removes the growth instead of hiding it.
clip_answer: About the same. With clipping at 1.0: 4.361; without: 4.295. The largest gradient norm without clipping was 76.6 (step 1,257), but the damage is done by many ordinary steps that each push the query and key weights a little further, which clipping does not touch. QK-norm without clipping: 2.432.
flat_meas: 2.267 without the shrink against 2.279 with it. {%flat_say%}
flat_say: The difference is smaller than the spread between two seeds of the default init (2.279 and 2.260): with 12 branches the √12 shrink does not measurably matter. It is a depth effect: the papers above report it at hundreds of millions of parameters and dozens of layers, where this page cannot run.

{%place_say%}
place_say: At this scale the two placements that normalise the branch output train worse than pre-norm, and the attention logits say why. With the output norm nothing normalises what attention reads, so q and k grow with the raw stream: the largest logit reaches 5,693 at lr 3e-3 (pre-norm: 58.2) and the loss stalls at 3.405. The sandwich does normalise its input, yet its logits still reach 241 at 3e-3 and 7,239 at 1e-2. Neither placement ships alone: OLMo 2 adds QK-norm to its output norm (its paper: "in isolation, neither of these changes yield good results, but together" they help), Gemma 2 adds soft-capping to its sandwich and Gemma 3 QK-norm; with QK-norm added, output norm reaches 2.506 (largest logit 15.3) and the sandwich 2.396 (largest logit 12.5). QK-norm does not rescue post-norm, whose failure is the gradient, not the logits: post-norm + QK-norm at 3e-3 ends at 6.011, the unigram level, with a largest logit of only 5.70. Pre-norm + QK-norm is the most robust row: 2.273, 2.302 and 2.476 across a tenfold range of rates. Kim et al.'s Peri-LN advantage (below) does not reproduce at 6 layers and 12M tokens; their runs are 400M to 3.2B parameters.
qk_gain_meas: in this page's QK-norm run at lr 3e-2 the mean |q| after the norm is 3.6 to 11.6 per layer and |k| 3.1 to 11.9 at the end (unit gains would give 5.66 for both), and the largest logit is 67.1, about 12 times the unit-gain ceiling.
qk_gain_short: In the tiny GPT trained with QK-norm at lr 3e-2 the largest logit is 67.1 against a unit-gain ceiling of 5.66
qk_meas: Measured. Without a fix the largest logit passes 1,000 by step 100 and peaks at 20,865 (step 510); the lowest layer entropy falls to 0.004 nats, one-hot attention. The loss never becomes non-finite: the run stalls at a held-out 4.295, between the bigram floor (3.616) and the unigram floor. With QK-norm and everything else identical the largest logit peaks at 69.9 and the run reaches 2.432. For scale, at the default lr 3e-3 the same model without QK-norm peaks at 58.2 and reaches 2.279; with QK-norm at 3e-3, 2.273.

After training (pre-norm: the root's reference run; post-norm lr 1e-3; sandwich and output norm lr 3e-3) pre-norm grows the most, 1.31 to 65.5; the sandwich reaches 47.6 and the output norm 34.1; post-norm ends at 24.6, set by its last norm's learned gain. spike_say: No run has a loss spike by this definition: at a 1,500-step scale the loss changes too smoothly. The gradient norm separates them: 9 spikes without a fix, 9 with z-loss, 5 with the cap, 0 with QK-norm, against 1 at the default rate; the ML-fundamentals root found the same ordering on a character-level model (QK-norm 0, z-loss no better than nothing).
z_answer: No. With z-loss the largest attention logit still reaches 24,895 (without: 20,865) and the run ends at 4.289 against 4.295. Mean log Z at the end: 8.52 with z-loss, 8.67 without. The two instabilities are different softmaxes; the ML-fundamentals root found the same on a character-level model (z-loss alone did not remove the gradient spikes, QK-norm did).
z_meas: Mean log Z on the probe batch starts at 8.37 (a uniform guess over 4,096 tokens has log Z = ln 4096 = 8.32 when the logits are near 0) and ends at 11.46 in the healthy run at lr 3e-3, at 8.67 in the high-rate run without a fix and at 8.52 with z-loss 1e-4. {%z_say%}
z_say: So at this scale z-loss 1e-4 barely moves log Z (8.52 against 8.67). In the healthy run log Z drifts up to 11.46, where the penalty is 1e-4 × 11.46<sup>2</sup> = 0.013 nats, under 1% of the loss: the pull is weak by design, and the drift it prevents shows up over long runs, at scale and in low precision (published), none of which a 1,500-step float32 run has. It also left the attention logits alone (section 4).
